name: Cochlear hair-cell electrical response
summary: Sound-driven motion of the cochlea bends hair-cell stereocilia, opens mechanically gated channels, and creates an electrical signal. Atlas treats this as a transduced signal rather than as a 440 Hz electrical replica of the acoustic carrier.

axis.notes: Electrical output of cochlear mechanotransduction; the acoustic carrier frequency is not assumed to be preserved one-to-one.

constraints: depends on cochlear mechanics and hair-cell transduction
no carrier-frequency identity is asserted by this manifest

mechanisms.description: Sound-induced cochlear motion bends stereocilia, opens pore-like channels, and produces an electrical signal in sensory hair cells.

relationships.description: A 440 Hz acoustic input is one possible sound stimulus; cochlear mechanics and hair-cell mechanotransduction convert sound-driven motion into an electrical response without implying an identical electrical carrier.
Hair-cell transduction produces electrical signaling that is conveyed onward by the auditory nerve.

sources.title: How Do We Hear?
sources.publisher: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD), NIH

evidence.derivation: NIDCD describes a mechanical-to-electrical transduction chain. Atlas therefore leaves the downstream electrical spectrum unspecified instead of copying the acoustic carrier frequency.
